inner_core.name: Inner Core
inner_core.description: A solid ball of iron and nickel at Earth's center, nearly at its melting point despite the crushing pressure.
inner_core.about: Temperatures near 5,400 degrees Celsius keep the inner core close to melting even under the weight of the whole planet. It turns slightly faster than the rest of Earth, which adds complexity to the magnetic field generated in the liquid layer above it.
inner_core.source: Dziewonski, A. M. & Anderson, D. L. (1981), "Preliminary reference Earth model", Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25:297-356 -- inner core boundary (ICB) at r = 1221.5 km.

outer_core.name: Outer Core
outer_core.description: A liquid layer of iron and nickel whose churning currents generate Earth's magnetic field.
outer_core.about: The outer core is molten iron and nickel with lighter elements mixed in, at 4,500 to 5,400 degrees Celsius. Convection in this conducting fluid acts as a dynamo, the geodynamo, and produces the magnetic field that reaches out into space to form the magnetosphere.
outer_core.source: Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), PREM, Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25:297-356 -- core-mantle boundary (CMB) at r = 3480 km.

lower_mantle.name: Lower Mantle
lower_mantle.description: The deep layer of hot, solid rock between the core and the upper mantle, flowing very slowly over millions of years.
lower_mantle.about: The lower mantle is solid silicate rock rich in iron and magnesium, at 2,200 to 4,500 degrees Celsius and under enormous pressure. Although solid, it creeps slowly by convection, and that slow flow is what drives the plates at the surface.
lower_mantle.source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, Earth -- volumetric mean radius; Ishii, T., Huang, R., Fei, H. et al. (2018), "Complete agreement of the post-spinel transition with the 660-km seismic discontinuity", Sci. Rep. 8:6358, doi:10.1038/s41598-018-24832-y -- section "New results of the post-spinel transition pressure in complete agreement with the discontinuity depth": the global average depth of the discontinuity is 660 +/- 10 km.

upper_mantle.name: Upper Mantle
upper_mantle.description: The rock beneath the crust, including the partly molten layer where most magma is born and on which the plates slide.
upper_mantle.about: The upper mantle includes the asthenosphere, a partly molten layer that flows more readily than the mantle below it, letting the tectonic plates move. It reaches from the base of the crust down to the top of the lower mantle, with temperatures from about 500 to 2,200 degrees Celsius.
upper_mantle.source: Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), PREM, Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25:297-356 -- base of the crust (Mohorovicic discontinuity) in the reference model, r = 6346.6 km.

crust.name: Crust
crust.description: Earth's thin, solid outer skin: the ground we live on, the ocean floors, and everything that has ever lived.
crust.about: The crust is thin compared with the planet: 5 to 10 km under the oceans, where it is mostly basalt, and 30 to 50 km under the continents, where it is mostly granite. Surface temperatures range from about minus 80 to 60 degrees Celsius. It holds all known life and every resource we can reach.
crust.source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, Earth -- volumetric mean radius
crust.source_note: The Earth radius used as the unit stays the IAU's equatorial one: Prsa et al. (2016), AJ 152:41, on IAU 2015 Resolution B3.
crust.note: Drawn at the mean radius, the sphere the interior layers (PREM) are measured against. Crust thickness (5-10 km oceanic, 30-50 km continental) is below the drawn resolution.
crust.radius_note: This is Earth's mean radius: the radius of a ball with the same volume as the smooth, slightly flattened shape fitted to sea level. The Earth radius used as a unit here is the equatorial radius, as the International Astronomical Union recommends, so the mean radius is a little less than one. The ground itself rises and falls from this by kilometres.

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

lower_atmosphere.name: Lower Atmosphere (to the stratopause)
lower_atmosphere.description: The air where weather happens and the ozone layer sits: the troposphere and stratosphere, holding nearly all the atmosphere's mass.
lower_atmosphere.about: The troposphere, the lowest 12 km or so, is where clouds and weather form; above it the stratosphere, to about 50 km, holds the ozone layer. Together they contain 99 percent of the atmosphere's mass, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Temperature falls from about 15 degrees Celsius at sea level to minus 60 at the top of the troposphere, then warms again toward the stratopause as ozone absorbs sunlight.

altitude.source: NOAA JetStream, "Layers of the Atmosphere" -- stratosphere to about 50 km; and NASA, "Earth's Atmospheric Layers" -- the stratosphere extends to 50 km.

lower_atmosphere.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1; NOAA JetStream, "Layers of the Atmosphere" -- stratosphere to about 50 km; and NASA, "Earth's Atmospheric Layers" -- the stratosphere extends to 50 km.
lower_atmosphere.note: Troposphere and stratosphere, 99% of atmospheric mass. Drawn at the physical boundary since 2026-09-07 (L-295); before that at a visibility fraction its own hover contradicted.

upper_atmosphere.name: Upper Atmosphere (to the thermopause)
upper_atmosphere.description: The thin upper air where meteors burn up, the aurora glows, and the Space Station orbits, fading toward space.
upper_atmosphere.about: Above 50 km lie the mesosphere, where most meteors burn up, the thermosphere, where the aurora appears and the International Space Station flies, and, higher still, the beginning of the exosphere. In the thermosphere the gas can reach 2,000 degrees Celsius, yet it is so thin it would feel cold to the skin.

altitude.source: NOAA JetStream, same page -- thermosphere from about 85 km to about 600 km, the exosphere beyond; NASA, same page -- the thermosphere extends to 600 km.

upper_atmosphere.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1; NOAA JetStream, same page -- thermosphere from about 85 km to about 600 km, the exosphere beyond; NASA, same page -- the thermosphere extends to 600 km.
upper_atmosphere.note: Mesosphere and thermosphere. The thermopause moves with solar activity over roughly 500-1,000 km; 600 km is the nominal figure.

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

geocorona.name: Exosphere / Geocorona (hydrogen halo, detected extent)
geocorona.description: A faint halo of hydrogen gas that surrounds Earth and thins out far into space, the outermost trace of the atmosphere.
geocorona.about: The exosphere has no top: it simply thins into space. Its hydrogen glows faintly in ultraviolet light, a halo called the geocorona. This shell is drawn where that glow has been detected, not where the atmosphere ends.
geocorona.source: Baliukin, I. I., Bertaux, J.-L., Quemerais, E., Izmodenov, V. V. & Schmidt, W. (2019), "SWAN/SOHO Lyman-alpha mapping: the hydrogen geocorona extends well beyond the Moon", J. Geophys. Res. Space Physics 124, 861-885, doi:10.1029/2018JA026136 -- the geocorona is detected to at least 100 Earth radii.
geocorona.note: The exosphere has no boundary: it thins into space. This shell is the sourced DETECTION FLOOR, not an edge, and it encloses the Moon's orbit at about 60 Earth radii.

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

leo_inner.name: Low Earth Orbit, inner edge (180 km)
leo_inner.description: The lower edge of low Earth orbit, the band of space where most satellites and the Space Station fly.
leo_inner.about: Low Earth orbit is the region from roughly 180 to 2,000 km up. Satellites there circle at every angle to the equator, so together they form a shell around Earth rather than a ring, and each completes an orbit in about 90 to 120 minutes. The International Space Station, the Hubble Space Telescope, Starlink and most weather and Earth-observing satellites live here; the moving lights seen at dusk and dawn are usually these.

radius_km.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1; ESA, "Types of orbits" (2020), section "Low Earth orbit (LEO)", https://www.esa.int/Our_Activities/Launchers/Types_of_orbits -- the lower limit for how low a satellite can fly is down to the impact of Earth's atmosphere; generally, satellites do not fly below 180 km for this reason.

altitude.source: ESA, "Types of orbits" (2020), section "Low Earth orbit (LEO)", https://www.esa.int/Our_Activities/Launchers/Types_of_orbits -- the lower limit for how low a satellite can fly is down to the impact of Earth's atmosphere; generally, satellites do not fly below 180 km for this reason.

leo_inner.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1; ESA, "Types of orbits" (2020), section "Low Earth orbit (LEO)", https://www.esa.int/Our_Activities/Launchers/Types_of_orbits -- the lower limit for how low a satellite can fly is down to the impact of Earth's atmosphere; generally, satellites do not fly below 180 km for this reason.
leo_inner.source_note: The region itself begins at the surface; the inner edge is drawn at the lowest height satellites fly.

leo_outer.name: Low Earth Orbit, outer edge (2,000 km)
leo_outer.description: The upper edge of low Earth orbit, about 2,000 km up, above which the sky belongs to higher orbits.
leo_outer.about: Low Earth orbit is the region from roughly 180 to 2,000 km up. Satellites there circle at every angle to the equator, so together they form a shell around Earth rather than a ring, and each completes an orbit in about 90 to 120 minutes. The International Space Station, the Hubble Space Telescope, Starlink and most weather and Earth-observing satellites live here; the moving lights seen at dusk and dawn are usually these.

radius_km.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1; IADC Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines, IADC-02-01 REVISION 2, March 2020, section 3.3.2 (1) -- the LEO Protected Region extends from the Earth's surface to an altitude of 2,000 km. Section 3.3.1 takes the equatorial radius as the reference surface and gives it as 6,378 km.

altitude.source: IADC Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines, IADC-02-01 REVISION 2, March 2020, section 3.3.2 (1) -- the LEO Protected Region extends from the Earth's surface to an altitude of 2,000 km. Section 3.3.1 takes the equatorial radius as the reference surface and gives it as 6,378 km.

leo_outer.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1; IADC Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines, IADC-02-01 REVISION 2, March 2020, section 3.3.2 (1) -- the LEO Protected Region extends from the Earth's surface to an altitude of 2,000 km. Section 3.3.1 takes the equatorial radius as the reference surface and gives it as 6,378 km.

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

geostationary_ring.name: Geostationary Belt (GEO)
geostationary_ring.description: A ring of satellites 35,786 km above the equator that circle exactly as fast as Earth turns, so each hangs over one spot.
geostationary_ring.about: Satellites in the geostationary belt orbit once a day, matching Earth's rotation, and so stay fixed over a point on the equator. Several hundred of them carry television, weather imagery and communications for much of the world. In April 2029 the asteroid Apophis will pass inside this ring, a few thousand kilometers below the nearest satellites.

radius_km.source: IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, Table 1.1 -- geocentric gravitational constant GM_E = 3.986004418e14 m^3 s^-2 (uncertainty 8e5 m^3 s^-2). IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, Table 1.2 "Parameters of the Geodetic Reference System GRS80" -- nominal mean Earth angular velocity, 7.292115e-5 rad s^-1. NASA Earth Observatory, Riebeek (2009, page updated 2025-11-14), "Catalog of Earth Satellite Orbits", section High Earth Orbit, https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/catalog-of-earth-satellite-orbits/ -- at 42,164 km from Earth's centre the orbit matches Earth's rotation, so a satellite seems to stay over a single longitude; circular and over the equator, it is geostationary.

geostationary_ring.hover: A ring in the equatorial plane, not a sphere: satellites here keep pace with Earth's turning and hang over one longitude.
geostationary_ring.source: IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, Table 1.1 -- geocentric gravitational constant GM_E = 3.986004418e14 m^3 s^-2 (uncertainty 8e5 m^3 s^-2). IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, Table 1.2 "Parameters of the Geodetic Reference System GRS80" -- nominal mean Earth angular velocity, 7.292115e-5 rad s^-1. NASA Earth Observatory, Riebeek (2009, page updated 2025-11-14), "Catalog of Earth Satellite Orbits", section High Earth Orbit, https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/catalog-of-earth-satellite-orbits/ -- at 42,164 km from Earth's centre the orbit matches Earth's rotation, so a satellite seems to stay over a single longitude; circular and over the equator, it is geostationary.
geostationary_ring.note: A ring in the equatorial plane, not a sphere, tilted with Earth's equator by the served pole. 42,164 km from Earth's centre, 35,786 km up.

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

params._comment: The orrery emits magnetopause, bow shock, inner belt and outer belt from ONE call. Served as four rows: the two standoffs here, the two belts in van_allen_belts. Renderer for the standoff shapes is step 3.

magnetopause.name: Magnetopause
magnetopause.description: The outer boundary of Earth's magnetic field, where it holds off the solar wind: pressed in by day, trailing a long tail by night.
magnetopause.about: Earth's magnetic field carves a cavity in the solar wind called the magnetosphere. On the side facing the Sun the wind presses it in; on the night side it stretches into a magnetotail observed far beyond the Moon's distance. The magnetopause is that boundary. It deflects the solar wind and turns aside many of the charged particles that reach Earth from the Sun and from beyond the solar system. The surface drawn is a model for a quiet solar wind; the real boundary moves in and out as the wind's pressure changes.

surface._model: Shue et al. (1998) eq. 10 with eq. 11. r = r0 [2 / (1 + cos theta)]^alpha, theta measured from the Sun-Earth line, r0 the standoff below. The geometry evaluates alpha = (a6 + a7 Bz)(1 + a8 ln Dp) from the rows here; alpha gets no row of its own because no text on the page prints it. At the declared conditions alpha is 0.59 -- two figures, because a6 is 0.58 +/- 0.01 and that carries straight through.

a6.source: Shue et al. (1998), doi:10.1029/98JA01103 -- Table 1 "After Fit" row a6, p. 17,698: 0.58 +/- 0.01. The leading term of eq. 11.

a8.source: Shue et al. (1998), doi:10.1029/98JA01103 -- Table 1 "After Fit" row a8, p. 17,698: 0.024 +/- 0.0004. The pressure term of eq. 11.

bz._declared: A neutral midpoint chosen for this scene, NOT a figure from the paper. Both boundaries are evaluated at the same conditions so the two surfaces can be compared.

pressure._declared: The solar wind dynamic pressure both fits are evaluated at. Declared for this scene, not measured.

cut_angle._declared: Where the drawn surface stops, measured from the nose. Shue's surface has no end: at this flaring the radius grows without bound as theta approaches 180 degrees, so a drawing must choose a stop. Shue et al. (1998) fig. 6, p. 17,695 plots the model out to 120 degrees, the furthest the authors evaluate it. A drawing limit, not an edge.

scatter.hover_line: Spacecraft that cross the real boundary typically find it within {value} Earth radii of this model.
scatter.source: Shue et al. (1998), doi:10.1029/98JA01103, p. 17,697 -- the improved model's standard deviation against the observed magnetopause crossings it was fitted to is 1.23 R_E.

magnetopause.hover:
Drawn to {cut_angle} deg from the nose, as far as the paper plots its model. Beyond that angle the boundary is drawn as the magnetotail.
Not tilted: the model is symmetric about the Sun line.
It is drawn along the line from the Sun to Earth; the real boundary's nose is turned a few degrees toward the direction Earth moves in its orbit, by an amount that depends on the solar wind's speed.
magnetopause.panel_words: Shue et al. (1998), for the solar wind assumed here: Bz {bz} nT, dynamic pressure {pressure} nPa.
magnetopause.source: Shue, J.-H., Song, P., Russell, C. T., Steinberg, J. T., Chao, J. K., Zastenker, G., Vaisberg, O. L., Kokubun, S., Singer, H. J., Detman, T. R. and Kawano, H. (1998), "Magnetopause location under extreme solar wind conditions", J. Geophys. Res. 103(A8), 17691-17700, doi:10.1029/98JA01103 -- Table 1 "After Fit" row a1, p. 17,698: 10.22 +/- 0.10 R_E. The leading term of eq. 10.; Shue et al. (1998), doi:10.1029/98JA01103 -- Table 1 "After Fit" row a2, p. 17,698: 1.29 +/- 0.06 R_E. The amplitude of eq. 10's Bz term.; Shue et al. (1998), doi:10.1029/98JA01103 -- Table 1 "After Fit" row a5, p. 17,698: 6.6 +/- 0.5. The pressure exponent, r0 varying as Dp^(-1/a5).; Shue et al. (1998), doi:10.1029/98JA01103 -- Table 1 "After Fit" row a3, p. 17,698: 0.184 +/- 0.007 per nT. The scale inside eq. 10's hyperbolic tangent.; Shue et al. (1998), doi:10.1029/98JA01103 -- Table 1 "After Fit" row a4, p. 17,698: 8.14 +/- 0.39 nT. The Bz offset inside eq. 10's hyperbolic tangent.
magnetopause.source_note: Shue's eq. 10, worked out at the solar wind chosen for the picture.
magnetopause.note: Quiet-time nominal. Under storm compression it can fall inside geostationary orbit (6.6 R_E).

bow_shock.name: Bow Shock
bow_shock.description: The shock wave where the supersonic solar wind first slows as it hits Earth's magnetic field, like the bow wave of a boat.
bow_shock.about: The solar wind moves faster than sound travels through the thin gas of space, so when it meets Earth's magnetic field it cannot flow smoothly around it: a standing shock forms upstream, sunward of the magnetopause, where the wind slows and heats. The surface drawn is a model for a quiet solar wind, and real crossings scatter around it.

surface._model: Jelinek et al. (2012), the paraboloid of eqs. 15-16 parameterised by tau: x = R0 p^(-1/eps) - tau^2 / 2, and the distance from the Sun-Earth line is sqrt(2 R0 p^(-1/eps)) tau / lambda. At tau = 0 this is the standoff below. A different functional form from the magnetopause because it is a different paper's fit, not a variation on Shue.

r0.source: Jelinek, K., Nemecek, Z. and Safrankova, J. (2012), "A new approach to magnetopause and bow shock modeling based on automated region identification", J. Geophys. Res. 117, A05208, doi:10.1029/2011JA017252 -- eq. 14, p. 5: R_BS = 15.02 p^(-1/6.55), so 15.02 R_E is the bow shock stand-off at p = 1 nPa. Fitted from Themis crossings, in aberrated GSE.

epsilon.source: Jelinek et al. (2012), doi:10.1029/2011JA017252 -- eq. 14, p. 5: the pressure exponent of R_BS = 15.02 p^(-1/6.55).

lambda.source: Jelinek et al. (2012), doi:10.1029/2011JA017252 -- sec. 4, in the text after eq. 11: lambda = 1.17 for the bow shock.

pressure._declared: The same declared pressure as the magnetopause. Both surfaces must be evaluated at the same conditions or their relative positions mean nothing.

cut_angle._declared: Where the drawn surface stops, measured from the nose. Jelinek et al. fitted crossings within 7 hours of local noon either side, and 7 hours of Earth's turn is 105 degrees. A drawing limit set by where the data was, not by where the formula fails -- the opposite reason from the magnetopause's 120.
cut_angle.source: Jelinek et al. (2012), doi:10.1029/2011JA017252 -- sec. 2 para. 9, p. 2: the regions are identified on the whole dayside and toward the flanks within +/- 7 hours of local time about local noon. That envelope is the extent over which the fit is supported.

scatter.hover_line: Spacecraft that cross the real shock typically find it within {value} Earth radii of this model.
scatter.source: Jelinek, Nemecek and Safrankova (2012), J. Geophys. Res. 117, A05208, doi:10.1029/2011JA017252 -- fig. 7: the scatter of observed crossings about the bow shock model is 0.69 R_E. The same figure gives 0.76 R_E for their magnetopause.

bow_shock.hover:
Drawn to {cut_angle} deg from the nose, which is how far round the crossings the fit was made from actually reached.
Not tilted: the fit is symmetric about the Sun line.
It is drawn along the line from the Sun to Earth; the real shock's nose is turned a few degrees toward the direction Earth moves in its orbit, by an amount that depends on the solar wind's speed.
bow_shock.panel_words: Jelinek et al. (2012), at dynamic pressure {pressure} nPa. Drawn to {cut_angle} deg from the nose: that is where the drawing stops, not where the shock ends.
bow_shock.source: Jelinek, K., Nemecek, Z. and Safrankova, J. (2012), "A new approach to magnetopause and bow shock modeling based on automated region identification", J. Geophys. Res. 117, A05208, doi:10.1029/2011JA017252 -- eq. 14, p. 5: R_BS = 15.02 p^(-1/6.55), so 15.02 R_E is the bow shock stand-off at p = 1 nPa. Fitted from Themis crossings, in aberrated GSE.; Jelinek et al. (2012), doi:10.1029/2011JA017252 -- eq. 14, p. 5: the pressure exponent of R_BS = 15.02 p^(-1/6.55).
bow_shock.source_note: Jelinek's eq. 14, worked out at the solar wind pressure chosen for the picture.
bow_shock.note: For a quiet solar wind, at the same pressure as the magnetopause.

magnetotail.name: Magnetotail
magnetotail.description: Earth's magnetic field, drawn out by the solar wind into a long tail on the night side.
magnetotail.about: The solar wind drags Earth's magnetic field out behind the planet into a long tail. Spacecraft crossing it far downstream found that it stops widening about 120 Earth radii behind Earth and is about 60 Earth radii across beyond there. ISEE-3 followed it out to 220 Earth radii, which is how far the spacecraft went rather than where the tail ends. The tail is drawn round, which is close to its shape on average; at any moment it is often flattened, in a direction set by the solar wind's own magnetic field, which keeps changing.
magnetotail._declared: The tail continues Shue's magnetopause surface from where the drawing of that surface stops, at the magnetopause's served cut angle; its starting distance and radius are worked out in the page from the served Shue rows, not served. From there it widens in a straight line to drawn_radius at flare_end, then keeps that radius to drawn_end, and it is round. flare_end and diameter are measurements; drawn_radius and drawn_end are rules over them, declared on their rows in constants_new.py, and the page uses them only for the shape. The five numbers the orrery's tail was drawn with until 2026-09-25 (100, 15 and 25 Earth radii, colour and opacity), which nothing in the gallery read, are gone (L-322 Stage D, gallery patch 3). color and opacity here are drawing choices, the magnetopause's, so the two read as one surface.

flare_end.hover_line: Spacecraft found the tail stops widening about {flare} Earth radii behind Earth, plus or minus {flare_unc}, and is about {width} Earth radii wide beyond there, plus or minus {width_unc}.
flare_end.source: Slavin, J. A., Smith, E. J., Sibeck, D. G., Baker, D. N., Zwickl, R. D. and Akasofu, S.-I. (1985), "An ISEE 3 study of average and substorm conditions in the distant magnetotail", J. Geophys. Res. 90(A11), 10875-10895, doi:10.1029/JA090iA11p10875 -- abstract: flaring ceases on average at |X| = 120 +/- 10 R_E.

diameter.source: Slavin et al. (1985), doi:10.1029/JA090iA11p10875 -- abstract: from 756 magnetopause crossings, a low-latitude magnetotail diameter of 60 +/- 5 R_E at |X| = 130 - 225 R_E.
diameter.note: Low-latitude: the crossings were near the plane of Earth's orbit, so this is the tail's width, side to side, not its height.

drawn_radius._declared: Half the measured diameter, the radius of the round tube the tail is drawn as beyond flare_end. A rule, not a measurement; its reasons are on the row in constants_new.py.
drawn_radius.source: Slavin et al. (1985), doi:10.1029/JA090iA11p10875 -- abstract: from 756 magnetopause crossings, a low-latitude magnetotail diameter of 60 +/- 5 R_E at |X| = 130 - 225 R_E.

drawn_end._declared: Where the drawing stops: equal to observed_extent, how far ISEE-3 went. A drawing limit, not an edge of anything physical.
drawn_end.source: Slavin, J. A., Tsurutani, B. T., Smith, E. J., Jones, D. E. and Sibeck, D. G. (1983), "Average configuration of the distant (less than 220-earth-radii) magnetotail - Initial ISEE-3 magnetic field results", Geophys. Res. Lett. 10(10), 973-976, doi:10.1029/GL010i010p00973, abstract open at https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19830066648 -- the abstract states that the magnetotail retains much of its near-Earth structure out to X = -220 Earth radii.

observed_extent.source: Slavin, J. A., Tsurutani, B. T., Smith, E. J., Jones, D. E. and Sibeck, D. G. (1983), "Average configuration of the distant (less than 220-earth-radii) magnetotail - Initial ISEE-3 magnetic field results", Geophys. Res. Lett. 10(10), 973-976, doi:10.1029/GL010i010p00973, abstract open at https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19830066648 -- the abstract states that the magnetotail retains much of its near-Earth structure out to X = -220 Earth radii.
observed_extent.note: Read as OBSERVED TO AT LEAST, not as an edge. 220 R_E is ISEE-3's reach on its first two tail passes, so the figure is bounded by the orbit rather than by where the tail ends. Two further signatures are more distant and less like a tail: Ness, Scearce and Cantarano (1967), doi:10.1029/JZ072i015p03769, report Pioneer 7 in the expected tail region at 900 to 1,050 R_E over a week in 1966, intermittently and with no coherent tail, the title saying 'probable'; and Intriligator et al. (1979), Geophys. Res. Lett. 6:585, report tail-ASSOCIATED phenomena near 3,100 R_E, read by later work as signatures disconnected from Earth.

magnetotail.hover:
The straight widening up to that point is our choice; the measurements give only its two ends.
The drawing stops at {observed_extent} Earth radii, which is how far the spacecraft went, not where the tail ends.
Drawn round, its average shape; at any moment it is often flattened.
magnetotail.source: Slavin et al. (1985), J. Geophys. Res. 90(A11):10875, doi:10.1029/JA090iA11p10875 -- ISEE-3: flaring ceases on average at 120 +/- 10 R_E behind Earth, and the tail is 60 +/- 5 R_E across beyond there. Slavin et al. (1983), Geophys. Res. Lett. 10(10):973, doi:10.1029/GL010i010p00973 -- observed to 220 R_E. The tail's shape: Sibeck and Lin (2014), J. Geophys. Res. Space Physics 119, doi:10.1002/2013JA019471 -- the distant tail is often flattened along the part of the solar wind's magnetic field that lies across the Sun-Earth line; Maezawa, Hori, Mukai, Saito, Yamamoto, Kokubun and Nishida (1997), Adv. Space Res. 20(4-5):949, doi:10.1016/S0273-1177(97)00503-6 -- GEOTAIL found the distant tail about the same size in both directions under average conditions.
magnetotail.note: The straight widening between where the Sun-facing surface stops and 120 Earth radii is our choice: the measurements give only its two ends.

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

magnetic_tilt.source: Alken et al. magnetic_tilt.note: Served so the hover can quote it. The rings are NOT tilted by it. They are drawn in the equatorial plane, which is the daily average of the magnetic one, because a tilted plane needs a direction as well as an angle and that direction turns once a day while this scene is frozen (L-231, Tony's ruling 2026-09-15).

params._frame: The edge rows below are geocentric distances in the geomagnetic equatorial plane, which is the frame their sources state. Tony's ruling, 2026-09-14 (L-323 ruling B, second amendment). The literature is mixed -- Y. X. Li et al. (2023) states the outer span in L shells and Baker et al. (2018) states it both ways -- so each row names the paper its figure follows and the frame travels with the row rather than with the block.

inner_belt_distance.source: Baker, D. N. et al. (2018), "Space Weather Effects in the Earth's Radiation Belts", Space Sci. Rev. 214:17, doi:10.1007/s11214-017-0452-7 -- sec. 2: inner-zone proton fluxes peak near geocentric r ~ 1.5 R_E.
inner_belt_distance.note: A flux PEAK, not an edge. The edges are their own rows below, as of 2026-09-14 (L-305 item 7); this note carried the span in prose until then, which is what let the served figure and the orrery's disagree.

inner_belt_inner_edge.source: Meredith, N. P., Horne, R. B., Kersten, T., Fraser, B. J. and Grew, R. S. (2014), "Global morphology and spectral properties of EMIC waves derived from CRRES observations", J. Geophys. Res. Space Physics 119, 5328-5342, doi:10.1002/2014JA020064, open full text at https://nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/507469/1/jgra51120.pdf -- introduction, first paragraph: the inner belt extends from about 1.1 to 2 Earth radii in the geomagnetic equatorial plane.
inner_belt_inner_edge.note: Koskinen and Kilpua (2022) sec. 1.1 corroborate 1.1 to 2 R_E but are NOT the source, because they state it for the inner ELECTRON belt and put the energetic protons over about 1.1 to 3 R_E. The figure matched and the scope did not.

inner_belt_outer_edge.source: Meredith et al. (2014), doi:10.1002/2014JA020064 -- introduction, first paragraph, the outer end of the same stated span.
inner_belt_outer_edge.note: Two rows rather than one span, because provenance is per number and the two edges do not move together.

outer_belt_distance.source: Li, X., Xiang, Z., Mei, Y., O'Brien, D., Brennan, D., Zhao, H., Baker, D. N. and Temerin, M. A. (2025), "A New Electron and Proton Radiation Belt Identified by CIRBE/REPTile-2 Measurements After the Magnetic Super Storm of 10 May 2024", J. Geophys. Res. Space Physics 130, e2024JA033504, doi:10.1029/2024JA033504 -- sec. 1: the outer radiation belt is most intense around L = 4 and 5.; Li et al. (2025), doi:10.1029/2024JA033504 -- sec. 1: the outer radiation belt is most intense around L = 4 and 5.
outer_belt_distance.source_note: the value drawn is our midpoint of that band
outer_belt_distance.note: A flux PEAK, not an edge. The unit is L, the McIlwain parameter, which equals geocentric distance in Earth radii only where a field line crosses the magnetic equator -- so any string printing this value says 'at the equator'. Baker et al. (2018) was removed from this citation on 2026-09-14: his figure 30 uses L* = 4.5 as a selected analysis location rather than a universal peak, and his span figure belongs on the edge row below.

outer_belt_band_low.source: Li, X., Xiang, Z., Mei, Y., O'Brien, D., Brennan, D., Zhao, H., Baker, D. N. and Temerin, M. A. (2025), "A New Electron and Proton Radiation Belt Identified by CIRBE/REPTile-2 Measurements After the Magnetic Super Storm of 10 May 2024", J. Geophys. Res. Space Physics 130, e2024JA033504, doi:10.1029/2024JA033504 -- sec. 1: the outer radiation belt is most intense around L = 4 and 5.

outer_belt_band_high.source: Li et al. (2025), doi:10.1029/2024JA033504 -- sec. 1: the outer radiation belt is most intense around L = 4 and 5.

outer_belt_inner_edge.source: Meredith et al. (2014), doi:10.1002/2014JA020064, open full text at https://nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/507469/1/jgra51120.pdf -- introduction, first paragraph: the outer belt extends from 3 to 7 R_E. Li, Tu, Selesnick and Huang (2024), "Modeling the contribution of precipitation loss to a radiation belt electron dropout observed by Van Allen Probes", J. Geophys. Res. Space Physics 129, e2023JA032171, doi:10.1029/2023JA032171, open full text at https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10578577 -- introduction, first paragraph, the same span independently.
outer_belt_inner_edge.note: The layer below is Paulikas and Blake (1979) with Baker et al. (1986) for Meredith, and Ganushkina et al. (2011) with Van Allen et al. (1958) for Li. Baker et al. (2018) sec. 2 gives the same inner edge from SAMPEX and reports it reaching L ~ 2.5 under strong driving.

outer_belt_outer_edge.source: Meredith et al. (2014), doi:10.1002/2014JA020064, and Li, Tu et al. (2024), doi:10.1029/2023JA032171 -- both state the outer belt extending to 7 Earth radii, in their introductions.
outer_belt_outer_edge.note: The measuring review disagrees on the outside and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved by silence: Baker et al. (2018) sec. 2 and 3.4 puts the outer zone at r ~ 3 to >= 6.5 R_E from SAMPEX and, in L, at about 3.0 to 6.5. Koskinen and Kilpua (2022) sec. 1.1 put the outer reach at 7 to 10 R_E, which is why an outer figure near 10 R_E is not the physical impossibility one checker called it -- the belt's outer edge approaches the magnetopause, and magnetopause shadowing is a standard loss mechanism.

descriptions: A belt of trapped charged particles, mostly protons, held by Earth's magnetic field close above the atmosphere.
A broader belt of trapped electrons farther out, that swells and shrinks with solar storms.
abouts: The inner Van Allen belt is a region of energetic protons trapped by Earth's magnetic field. The particles are held along the field lines, so the belt curves down toward the ground on either side of the equator. The real field is tilted from Earth's axis and turns with Earth once a day; the belt drawn here follows the field's daily average, lined up with the spin axis.

The outer Van Allen belt is mostly energetic electrons, trapped farther out than the inner belt, and it swells and shrinks as the solar wind changes. Like the inner belt it is held along the field lines, which meet the ground nearer the poles; it is drawn around the field's daily average, lined up with the spin axis.
hovers_band: Thickest at {drawn} Earth radii: halfway across the band, {low} to {high} Earth radii out at the magnetic equator, where the belt is most intense. The halfway point is our choice for the picture, not a measured peak.
hovers_shape: The belt is one continuous region. Its dots follow Earth's magnetic field lines, which curve from the equator down toward the ground, and they are thickest where the belt is most intense. How they thin out is drawn to show the shape, not measured.

The belt is one continuous region. Its dots follow Earth's magnetic field lines, which curve from the equator down toward the ground, and they are thickest where the belt is most intense. How they thin out is drawn to show the shape, not measured.
hovers_plane: The field lines are drawn around Earth's spin axis: the daily average of the magnetic field, which turns with Earth and in 2020 was tilted {tilt} degrees from it{rate} (IGRF-13 model). The belt stops where its field lines meet the ground.

The field lines are drawn around Earth's spin axis: the daily average of the magnetic field, which turns with Earth and in 2020 was tilted {tilt} degrees from it{rate} (IGRF-13 model). The belt stops where its field lines meet the ground.

drawing._declared: Not a number: the name of the stored drawing the belts are, data/solar-system/drawings/van_allen_belts.json. The orrery places the dots (van_allen_belt_sampler.py, from the six belt rows above) and the page draws them as given (L-330, Tony's rulings of 2026-10-17; the stored-drawing rule of L-421).

params._declared: colours, names and info_borders are drawing choices; info_borders mirrors the orrery's two-standards outline (shell_configs.py). Each belt is the stored drawing named under drawing: dots scattered at random along dipole field lines between its served edges, thickest at its served peak, each shaded by its weight. The orrery places them and the page scales them by planet_radius and turns them to Earth's pole; how the dots look is a rendering setting in gallery/feature_renderers.js. Until 2026-10-17 each belt was drawn as evenly spaced rings in the equatorial plane (L-322 Stage D, gallery patch 3), and n_points still sets the rings' points for a body drawn that way. L-330.

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

hill_sphere.name: Hill Sphere (gravitational dominance over the Sun)
hill_sphere.description: The region where Earth's gravity, not the Sun's, is the stronger hold; the Moon orbits well inside it.
hill_sphere.about: Inside the Hill sphere a body can orbit Earth without being pulled away by the Sun. The Moon lies deep within it. Beyond this sphere the Sun's gravity wins, and an object would drift into its own orbit around the Sun.

radius_km.source: IAU 2012 Resolution B2 -- exact definition; IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, Table 1.1 -- geocentric gravitational constant GM_E = 3.986004418e14 m^3 s^-2 (uncertainty 8e5 m^3 s^-2).; IAU 2015 Resolution B3, published as Prsa et al. (2016), AJ 152, 41, doi:10.3847/0004-6256/152/2/41.

hill_sphere.source: IAU 2012 Resolution B2 -- exact definition; IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, Table 1.1 -- geocentric gravitational constant GM_E = 3.986004418e14 m^3 s^-2 (uncertainty 8e5 m^3 s^-2).; IAU 2015 Resolution B3, published as Prsa et al. hill_sphere.note: About 1.50 million km. The Moon at about 60 Earth radii sits well inside it, which is why it stays bound. a = 1 AU exactly; Earth's semi-major axis is 1.00000011 AU (NASA Earth Fact Sheet).

ra.source: IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, sec. 2.1.1 -- the ICRS principal plane is held close to the mean equator at J2000.0, and the mean pole at J2000.0 sits 17.1 mas toward 12h and 5.0 mas toward 18h from the ICRS pole (IERS 1996 nutation), or 16.6 mas and 6.8 mas (MHB2000): about 0.02 arcseconds, some five millionths of a degree. The Horizons manual: the ICRF was built to align with FK5/J2000 and differs from it by at most 0.02 arcseconds.

rotation_period.hover_line: Earth turns once every {value} hours measured against the stars.
rotation_period.source: NIST Special Publication 811, Guide for the Use of the SI, sec. 5.1.1, Table 6 (units the CIPM accepts for use with the SI) -- the hour is 60 minutes, 3600 seconds, by definition.; IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, Table 1.2 "Parameters of the Geodetic Reference System GRS80" -- nominal mean Earth angular velocity, 7.292115e-5 rad s^-1.

params.source: The pole the room draws is Earth's north pole on the scene's date from JPL Horizons (observer quantity 32, target 399), served by the cache builder as pole_of_date. The pole here is the FALLBACK, drawn only when no pole of date is served: the z-axis of the ICRF, which IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, sec. 2.1.1, holds within about 0.02 arcseconds of Earth's mean pole at J2000.0, and which the Horizons manual's reference frames section describes as aligned with FK5/J2000 to that level. The IAU working group report (Archinal et al. 2018) was cited here until 2026-09-26; it gives no pole for Earth and sends users to the IERS.
params.note: Same shape as the Sun's orientation block; read by poleBasis(). The equator plane and the GEO ring both hang off this. rotation_period is quoted in the axis hover (L-322 Stage D, gallery patch 3).

words._comment: L-421 (2026-10-06): the sentences the Earth room's drawn guides state about nature -- the axis, the Sun line, the terminator, the Moon's arc -- served here with their sources, because the guides are drawn from this block and the scene's moment rather than from a shell of their own. gallery/earth_geometry.js prints each hover as given; {name} is a value it fills in from the scene. Each guide's link is its entry's info_url: the axis's on sense, the Sun line's on subsolar, the Moon group's on moon_arc (chosen 2026-10-06, every one a URL a search returned that day; no NASA page is specific to any of the four, so each is its Wikipedia article).

sense.hover: The curved arrows at both ends show the sense of the turning: prograde, west to east, counter-clockwise seen from above the north pole.
sense.source: Sense of rotation: Archinal et al. (2019), Correction to: Report of the IAU Working Group on Cartographic Coordinates and Rotational Elements: 2015, Cel. Mech. Dyn. Astron. 131:61, doi:10.1007/s10569-019-9925-1 -- Fig. 1 caption: a body whose prime-meridian angle W increases with time rotates prograde. Earth's turning: U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department, Glossary (consistent with The Astronomical Almanac 2023), https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/asa_glossary -- 'diurnal motion': the apparent daily motion of the sky from east to west is caused by Earth's rotation, so Earth turns west to east; 'direct motion': counterclockwise as seen from the north pole of the ecliptic, west to east -- the sense Earth's turning shares, so it is prograde. The two entries' wording is the Explanatory Supplement to the Astronomical Almanac's (Seidelmann 1992), checked against it 2026-10-06. The 2018 report (Cel. Mech. Dyn. Astron. 130:22) was cited here until 2026-10-06; its sections 2 and 7 were not re-read that day, so the citation moved to what was.

tilt_of_date.hover: Tilt: {tilt} deg on {date}, measured against the orbit of the Earth-Moon barycenter, the gravitational center of the Earth-Moon system, around the Sun that day (JPL Horizons).

tilt.hover: The axis slowly circles over thousands of years and nods slightly, so the pole and the tilt belong to that date.
tilt.source: U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department, Glossary (consistent with The Astronomical Almanac 2023), https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/asa_glossary -- 'precession': the smoothly changing orientation of Earth's equator, driven by the Sun and Moon pulling on the equatorial bulge; 'nutation': oscillations of the rotation pole; 'true equator and equinox' of a date, which both affect. Williams (1994), Contributions to the Earth's obliquity rate, precession, and nutation, Astron. J. 108:711, doi:10.1086/117108 -- sec. 1 and 5: precession of about 50 arcseconds a year, one full circle in roughly 26,000 years. Both read 2026-10-06.

subsolar.hover: The dot where the line leaves the crust is the subsolar point, where the Sun is overhead.
subsolar.source: U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department, Glossary (consistent with The Astronomical Almanac 2023), https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/asa_glossary -- 'sub-solar point': the point on a body's surface directly beneath the Sun, on the line from the body's centre to the Sun's; for a round body the Sun is at the zenith there. Read 2026-10-06.

terminator.hover:
The white circle is where the Sun is on the horizon: the sunlit half of Earth faces the Sun line, the night half faces away. The yellow line through the circle's centre is the Sun direction; its dot on the crust is the subsolar point, where the Sun is overhead.

FROZEN at {epoch}. The real terminator sweeps around Earth once a day; this scene does not turn. Geometry only -- no lighting is modelled, and the refraction and solar-disc corrections that define sunrise on the ground are not applied.
terminator.source: The terminator, 'the boundary between the illuminated and dark areas of a body', and the subsolar point: U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department, Glossary (consistent with The Astronomical Almanac 2023), https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/asa_glossary. Sunrise and its corrections: U.S. Naval Observatory, Rise, Set, and Twilight Definitions, https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/RST_defs -- Earth's rotation once a day causes rising and setting; sunrise is when the Sun's upper edge meets the horizon, its centre 50 arcminutes below it, 16 for the Sun's apparent radius and 34 for refraction. Both read 2026-10-06.

moon_arc.hover: The faint full ellipse is the same orbit swept once around; outside the arc, the Moon's real path drifts from it as the Sun and Earth's shape perturb the two-body orbit.
moon_arc.source: Williams (1994), Astron. J. 108:711, doi:10.1086/117108 -- sec. 1: strong solar torques drive the precession of the lunar orbit's plane, and Earth's oblateness adds a small torque; sec. 2: the lunar orbit is strongly perturbed by the Sun. U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department, Glossary (consistent with The Astronomical Almanac 2023), https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/asa_glossary -- 'osculating elements': the two-body orbit a body would follow if perturbations ceased. Both read 2026-10-06.

tilt.derived: the angle between Earth's pole of date and the pole of the Earth-Moon barycenter's orbit of date, both turned into the ecliptic of J2000 by the frame angle
